newsitem.title: USA: Icy rivers rage across northern U.S. plains.
newsitem.headline: Icy rivers rage across northern U.S. plains.

text.p: Rivers overflowing from melting snow raged across the northern U.S. plains on Wednesday, sending residents scrambling to reinforce barricades in hope of holding back the worst floods in more than 30 years.
In eastern Minnesota, parts of downtown Stillwater were below the level of the rushing St. Croix River, protected only by a temporary dike.
"It's a constant battle," said Stillwater city engineer Klayton Eckles. "We built the dike Saturday and Sunday and we've been reinforcing and patching since."
The rising river lapped against an historic bridge as tourists gawked at the sight from a nearby cafe.
"Where else can you eat in a restaurant that's no longer on the river but in the river?" cafe manager Carol Spoo said, surveying her waterlogged parking lot and garden.
The St. Croix was rushing to its juncture with the equally swollen Mississippi River 25 miles (40 km) south.

"Not only do we have to contend with melting snow, we have high water in the Mississippi that is causing backwash into the St. Croix and Minnesota Rivers," National Weather Service hydrologist Gary McDevitt said.

The St. Croix, which forms Minnesota's border with Wisconsin, was not expected to crest until Sunday, at about the same time the Mississippi was scheduled to crest in the nearby state capital of St. Paul.

Record-cold temperatures below zero (-18 C) at night have slowed the thaw, but made conditions difficult for the thousands stacking sandbags. Frozen sandbags are less malleable and provide a less binding seal.
The cold weather extended as far south as the Ohio River Valley and plunged to a record 15 degrees (-9 C) in Cincinnati, damaging fruit crops starting to bloom.
Temperatures were expected to remain below freezing in the flood-stricken northern plains through the middle of next week.
Vice President Al Gore will inspect storm and flood damage in Minnesota and the Dakotas on Friday, his office announced.
North Dakota Sen. Kent Conrad, a Democrat, praised Gore's decision to visit the diaster zones, saying it "will help energise the relief effort."

In St. Paul, inmates from the Ramsey County jail were helping build a six-foot (two metre) sand wall to protect their jailhouse and a government office building from the Mississippi. Tiny Harriet Island, which sits midstream, was flooded for the first time since 1965.

Another tributary, the Minnesota River, continued to create misery in south-central Minnesota, forcing some families out of their homes as it crested in New Ulm. The river was nearly one mile (1.6 km) across at New Ulm, compared to its normal 100 yards (metres).

"It's running very, very fast and the water is quite cold -- about 35 degrees (1.6 C)," New Ulm city council president Dan Beranek said. "We've told people stay the hell away from the river because it's dangerous."
About 40 homes in New Ulm could be swamped and National Guard troops were keeping a close eye on hastily built temporary dikes and sandbag walls, he said.
At least 1,000 residents of Ada, Minnesota, along the Wild Rice and Marsh Rivers, were driven from flooded homes and thousands were homeless in rural Minnesota and the Dakotas.

The false sense of ease caused by a lull in the spring thaw was broken on Wednesday in Fargo, North Dakota, when officials predicted the adjacent Red River would crest a foot (30 cm) higher than previously expected. An added worry was an ice jam that formed during recent frigid nights could unleash a wave of water in a river whose volume was already 10 times above normal.

Dakotas residents were given one reprieve -- the U.S. Internal Revenue Service said it would postpone their tax filing deadline to May 30 from April 15. But those owing money would have to pay nine percent annual interest.
